lesson.title: When Overdamped Means Overcautious: Two Real Roots
lesson.summary: An overdamped second order circuit returns to equilibrium using two decaying exponentials instead of a single one, and the slower of the two roots quietly controls how long the whole event takes.
lesson.body:
An overdamped response is what you get whenever the damping coefficient alpha exceeds the natural frequency omega0, equivalently whenever the damping ratio zeta = alpha/omega0 is greater than 1. In that regime the characteristic equation s^2 + 2 alpha s + omega0^2 = 0 has two real, distinct, negative roots, s1 = -alpha + sqrt(alpha^2 - omega0^2) and s2 = -alpha - sqrt(alpha^2 - omega0^2), and the general solution is a sum of two pure exponential decays, x(t) = A1 e^(s1 t) + A2 e^(s2 t). There is no sine or cosine anywhere in that expression, which is the whole point: an overdamped circuit has so much resistance relative to its natural frequency that it cannot complete even one oscillation before the energy is gone.

The two roots are not equally important. s1, the less negative of the two, decays more slowly and is called the dominant root, because after enough time it is the only term left with any appreciable size. s2 decays away almost immediately. This is why overdamped step responses in real systems, like an overdamped door closer or a heavily damped voltmeter needle, look sluggish: the fast term dies out quickly, but the slow term drags the tail of the response out for a comparatively long time. Engineers who need a fast, non-oscillating response usually push a design toward critical damping instead, precisely to avoid that long dominant-root tail.

Return to the series RLC circuit from the previous chapter, R = 40 ohms, L = 4 H, C = 1/64 F, which gave alpha = 5 rad/s, omega0 = 4 rad/s, and characteristic roots s1 = -2 rad/s and s2 = -8 rad/s. Suppose the source free current starts at i(0) = 0 A with an initial rate of change i'(0) = -6 A/s, set by the initial capacitor voltage and inductor current through the loop equation. The general solution is i(t) = A1 e^(-2t) + A2 e^(-8t). Applying i(0) = 0 gives A1 + A2 = 0, so A2 = -A1. Differentiating, i'(t) = -2A1 e^(-2t) - 8A2 e^(-8t), and applying i'(0) = -6 gives -2A1 - 8A2 = -6. Substituting A2 = -A1 turns this into -2A1 + 8A1 = 6A1 = -6, so A1 = -1 and A2 = 1.

The full solution is i(t) = -e^(-2t) + e^(-8t) amperes. Check both conditions directly: at t = 0, i(0) = -1 + 1 = 0, matching the given initial current. The derivative is i'(t) = 2e^(-2t) - 8e^(-8t), and at t = 0 that gives 2 - 8 = -6 A/s, matching the given initial slope. Both constants check out, confirming the solution is correct, not just plausible.

Notice how directly this all traces back to the damping ratio: zeta = 1.25 told us in advance, before solving anything, that the roots would be real and the response would be non-oscillatory. That predictive power is exactly why damping ratio and the alpha versus omega0 comparison from second order circuits are worth memorizing. They let you sketch the qualitative shape of a response, decaying smoothly to zero with no ringing, before you ever touch the algebra of initial conditions.
